decks.title: Indefinite Integrals — Part 1: Standard forms and powers of sine and cosine
goals: Describe integration as the reverse of differentiation and explain the constant of integration
Use the standard integrals of powers, the reciprocal, the exponential and the six trigonometric derivatives
Integrate functions of a linear expression ax + b
Integrate the squares, cubes and fourth powers of sine and cosine

slides.heading: Indefinite Integrals, Part 1
slides.body_md: Differentiation tells you the slope from the curve. Integration asks the opposite question.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: start from differentiation, read the results backwards to get the standard integrals, then integrate powers of sine and cosine.
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to indefinite integrals. So far you have found the derivative of a function. Now we run the process backwards: given a derivative, we look for the function it came from. In this part we build a table of standard integrals and learn to integrate powers of sine and cosine.

slides.heading: What you will learn
bullets: **Standard integrals** and a linear inside $ax + b$
Powers of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ up to the fourth

visual.alt: Table of standard integrals obtained by reading derivatives backwards: power of a linear expression, one over x gives log of mod x, e to the x, sine, cosine, secant squared and cosecant squared.
visual.caption: Each row is a derivative read from right to left.

slides.narration: Here are the goals. You will meet integration as anti-differentiation, see why every answer carries a constant, build the standard results by reading derivatives backwards, handle expressions of the form a x plus b, and integrate powers of sine and cosine up to the fourth power.

slides.heading: Anti-differentiation and the constant C
slides.body_md: If $F'(x) = f(x)$, then $\displaystyle\int f(x)\,dx = F(x) + C$. Two antiderivatives of $f$ on an interval differ by a constant.

visual.alt: Graph of three parabolas y equals x squared minus 2, x squared, and x squared plus 2, one above another. At x equals 1 they pass through (1, minus 1), (1, 1) and (1, 3), and all three have the same slope 2 there.
visual.caption: Every member of $x^2 + C$ has derivative $2x$: the curves are vertical shifts of one another.

slides.narration: If F has derivative f, we call F an antiderivative of f. Adding any constant does not change the derivative, so the indefinite integral is a whole family of curves, F of x plus C. The three parabolas in the graph are shifted copies of one another, and at the same x they all have the same slope.

slides.heading: Standard integrals from derivatives
slides.body_md: Every derivative you know, read from right to left, is an integral.

visual.alt: Table of standard integrals obtained by reading derivatives backwards: power of a linear expression, one over x gives log of mod x, e to the x, sine, cosine, secant squared and cosecant squared.
visual.caption: Each row is a derivative read from right to left.

slides.narration: Each standard integral is simply a derivative read backwards. Because the derivative of log of mod x is one over x, the integral of one over x is log of mod x. Because the derivative of minus cos x is sin x, the integral of sin x is minus cos x. Learn this table well: every later method reduces to it.

slides.heading: Quick check: an exponential
slides.body_md: Choose the integral of an exponential with a linear exponent.
slides.narration: Differentiate each option in your head. Which one gives back exactly the integrand?

slides.heading: A linear inside: ax + b
slides.body_md: If $\displaystyle\int f(x)\,dx = F(x) + C$, then $\displaystyle\int f(ax + b)\,dx = \dfrac1a F(ax + b) + C$.

visual.alt: Table of four integrands with a linear inside and their integrals: five x plus two cubed, e to the four minus three x, cosine of two x plus one, and one over three x minus four; in each case divide by the coefficient of x.
visual.caption: A linear inside $ax + b$ costs a factor $\dfrac1a$.

slides.narration: When the variable appears inside as a x plus b, integrate as usual and then divide by a, the coefficient of x. The chain rule would multiply by a when differentiating, so integration must divide by it. The table shows four examples with powers, exponentials, cosine and a reciprocal.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: expand, then integrate
slides.body_md: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{(x^2 + 1)^2}{x^2}\,dx$ for $x \ne 0$.
bullets: Integrate term by term with the power rule

visual.alt: Worked example table: expand x squared plus one, all squared, over x squared into x squared plus two plus x to the minus two, integrate term by term, and get x cubed over three plus two x minus one over x plus C.
visual.caption: Checked by differentiating back at four sample points.

slides.narration: There is no rule for a quotient, so first rewrite. Expanding the square and dividing by x squared gives three simple powers. Each power integrates with the power rule. The last term, x to the minus two, becomes minus one over x. Differentiate your answer to check it.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: using a condition
slides.body_md: An imagined tea stall has marginal profit $P'(x) = 40 - 6x$ (hundred rupees per hundred cups) and $P(0) = -50$. Find $P(x)$.

visual.alt: Table of the profit P of x equals 40 x minus 3 x squared minus 50 for an imagined tea stall at 0, 1, 3 and 5 hundred cups: minus 50, minus 13, 43 and 75 hundred rupees.
visual.caption: Imagined figures, in hundred rupees; the constant comes from $P(0) = -50$.

slides.narration: A condition fixes the constant. Integrate the marginal profit to get forty x minus three x squared plus K. When no cups are sold the stall loses fifty, so K is minus fifty. Now the profit formula is complete, and five hundred cups give a profit of seventy five hundred rupees.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false?
slides.body_md: Decide whether a claimed integral of an exponential is correct.
slides.narration: Differentiate the claimed answer. Does it give the original function, or a multiple of it?

slides.heading: Powers of sine and cosine
slides.body_md: Even powers: lower the power with a double-angle identity. Odd powers: keep one factor for a substitution.

visual.alt: Table of the six powers of sine and cosine in the syllabus: squares use the double-angle identity, cubes keep one factor for a substitution, and fourth powers use the double-angle identity twice; each row gives the rewrite and the integral.
visual.caption: Even powers: lower the power. Odd powers: keep one factor aside.

slides.narration: The syllabus asks for squares, cubes and fourth powers of sine and cosine. For even powers use the double-angle identities to turn them into first powers of cosines of multiple angles. For odd powers, keep one factor aside and write the rest using the other function; a substitution then finishes the job.

slides.heading: Squares of sine
slides.body_md: $\sin^2 x = \dfrac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}$, so $\displaystyle\int \sin^2 x\,dx = \dfrac{x}{2} - \dfrac{\sin 2x}{4} + C$.

visual.alt: Graph on 0 to about 6.3 of y equals sine squared x, which rises and falls between 0 and 1, and of its antiderivative x over 2 minus sine 2 x over 4, which climbs steadily, flattening wherever sine squared x is zero.
visual.caption: The antiderivative rises fastest where $\sin^2 x = 1$ and levels off where $\sin^2 x = 0$.

slides.narration: The square of sine is never negative, so its antiderivative never decreases. The graph shows the antiderivative climbing steadily and flattening wherever sine squared is zero. The formula comes from the identity sine squared equals one minus cos two x, all over two.

slides.heading: Quick check: the identity for sine squared
slides.body_md: Fill in the missing number in the integral of sine squared.
slides.narration: Integrate cos two x over two carefully. What do you divide by?

slides.heading: Odd powers: keep one factor
slides.body_md: $\cos^3 x = (1 - \sin^2 x)\cos x$; put $t = \sin x$.

visual.alt: Flow for an odd power of cosine: keep one factor of cos x aside, write the rest with sine using cos squared equals one minus sin squared, substitute t equals sin x, and integrate a polynomial in t.
visual.caption: The same steps work for $\sin^3 x$ with $t = \cos x$.

slides.narration: For an odd power, set one factor aside. The remaining even power can be written using the other function. Then substitute: with t equal to sin x, the saved cos x dx becomes d t, and you integrate a simple polynomial in t. The same plan works for sine cubed with t equal to cos x.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: an odd power of sine
slides.body_md: Find $\displaystyle\int \cos^2 x\sin^3 x\,dx$.
bullets: Keep one $\sin x$: $\cos^2 x(1 - \cos^2 x)\sin x$

visual.alt: Worked example table for cos squared x times sin cubed x: keep one sin x, write the rest with cosine, substitute t equals cos x with dt equals minus sin x dx, and get minus cos cubed x over three plus cos to the fifth x over five plus C.
visual.caption: Checked by differentiating back.

slides.narration: Sine has the odd power, so keep one sine aside and write sine squared as one minus cos squared. Substituting t equal to cos x turns the sine dx into minus d t. Integrate the polynomial, remember the minus sign, and write the answer back in terms of cos x.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a fourth power
slides.body_md: Find $\displaystyle\int \cos^4 x\,dx$.

visual.alt: Table comparing cos to the fourth x with three eighths plus half cos 2 x plus one eighth cos 4 x at x equals 0.3, 1 and 2: the two columns agree to four decimal places.
visual.caption: The reduction is an identity: both columns agree.

slides.narration: A fourth power needs the double-angle identity twice. Square the half-angle form, then lower cos squared two x once more. The result is a constant plus first powers of cos two x and cos four x, each easy to integrate. The table confirms the reduction at three values of x.

slides.heading: Quick check: reducing a fourth power
slides.body_md: Which identity starts the reduction of sine to the fourth power?
slides.narration: You need an identity that turns a square of sine into a first power of a cosine.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Even powers: double-angle identity (twice for fourth powers)
Odd powers: keep one factor and substitute

nodes.label: Odd powers: keep one factor, substitute

visual.alt: Summary flow for Part 1: standard integrals come from derivatives read backwards, a linear inside costs a factor one over a, even powers of sine and cosine use the double-angle identity, and odd powers keep one factor for a substitution.
visual.caption: Part 1 in one line.

slides.narration: To sum up. An integral is a family of antiderivatives, so always add a constant. Standard integrals are derivatives read backwards, and a linear inside costs a factor of one over a. Even powers of sine and cosine are lowered with double-angle identities; odd powers keep one factor for a substitution.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Divide by the coefficient of $x$ for $ax + b$
State the identity before using it

rows: correct form and the factor $\dfrac1a$; "$+\,C$" expected
general integral 1, constant from the condition 1, final answer 1
identity or rewrite 1, integration 1, simplified answer 1
differentiate your answer: it must give the integrand

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 1: a standard integral needs the right form and the factor one over a with plus C; a condition earns marks for the general integral, the constant and the final answer; powers earn a mark for the identity; always differentiate to check.
visual.caption: ISC marking follows the steps.

slides.narration: In the board examination, marks follow the steps. Always write plus C. Divide by the coefficient of x when the inside is linear. When you use an identity, write it down, because it often earns a mark. And before moving on, differentiate your answer to make sure it gives back the integrand.

decks.title: Indefinite Integrals — Part 2: Integration by substitution
goals: Choose a suitable substitution by spotting an inside function and its derivative
Integrate the forms f′(x)[f(x)]^n and f′(x)/f(x)
Derive the integrals of tan x, cot x, sec x and cosec x
Use substitution with roots, exponentials and logarithms

slides.heading: Indefinite Integrals, Part 2
slides.body_md: The chain rule, read backwards, is the method of substitution.

visual.alt: Route map of substitution: spot an inside function, call it t, find dt, integrate in t, and write the answer back in x.
visual.caption: Substitution is the chain rule read backwards.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Many integrands contain a function together with its derivative. Substitution turns them into simple standard integrals. We will learn to spot such patterns, derive the integrals of tan, cot, sec and cosec, and practise with roots, exponentials and logarithms.

slides.heading: What you will learn

visual.alt: Table of four substitution forms: f prime times f to the power n integrates to f to the n plus one over n plus one; f prime over f gives log of mod f; f prime times e to the f gives e to the f; f prime times cos f gives sin f.
visual.caption: Look for an inside function whose derivative is also present.

slides.narration: Here are the goals. You will learn the method of substitution, recognise the two most important patterns, derive the four trigonometric integrals, and build the judgement to choose a good substitution quickly.

slides.heading: The method of substitution
slides.body_md: If $t = g(x)$, then $dt = g'(x)\,dx$ and $\displaystyle\int f(g(x))\,g'(x)\,dx = \int f(t)\,dt$.

visual.alt: Route map of substitution: spot an inside function, call it t, find dt, integrate in t, and write the answer back in x.
visual.caption: Substitution is the chain rule read backwards.

slides.narration: The idea is to rename an inside function as t. Its derivative, multiplied by d x, becomes d t. If the integrand contains both the inside function and its derivative, everything can be written in t, and the new integral is usually a standard one. At the end, write t back in terms of x.

slides.heading: Two key patterns
slides.body_md: Look for the derivative of an inside function.

visual.alt: Table of four substitution forms: f prime times f to the power n integrates to f to the n plus one over n plus one; f prime over f gives log of mod f; f prime times e to the f gives e to the f; f prime times cos f gives sin f.
visual.caption: Look for an inside function whose derivative is also present.

slides.narration: Two patterns appear again and again. In the first, the derivative of a bracket multiplies a power of that bracket; the power rule finishes it. In the second, the numerator is the derivative of the denominator, and the answer is the log of the modulus of the denominator.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a power of a bracket
slides.body_md: Find $\displaystyle\int (2x + 3)(x^2 + 3x - 1)^5\,dx$.

visual.alt: Worked example table: for two x plus three times x squared plus three x minus one to the fifth, put t equal to the bracket, note dt equals two x plus three dx is present, integrate t to the fifth and get the bracket to the sixth over six plus C.
visual.caption: Checked by differentiating back at three points.

slides.narration: Look at the bracket: its derivative is two x plus three, which is exactly the other factor. So put t equal to the bracket. The whole integrand becomes t to the fifth times d t. The power rule gives t to the sixth over six, and then we put the bracket back.

slides.heading: Quick check: a constant to find
slides.body_md: Find the number that makes a substitution result correct.
slides.narration: Find d t for the bracket and see what extra factor is needed.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: numerator equals derivative
slides.body_md: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x}{x^2 + 4}\,dx$ and two more of the same type.

visual.alt: Table of three f prime over f integrals: x over x squared plus four is half of f prime over f and gives half log of x squared plus four; cos x over three plus sin x and e to the x over e to the x plus one are exactly f prime over f.
visual.caption: Adjust a constant factor when the numerator is a multiple of $f'$.

slides.narration: Compare the numerator with the derivative of the denominator. Here the numerator is half of it, so the answer is half the log of the denominator. Because x squared plus four is always positive, the modulus can be dropped. The table shows two more integrands where the numerator is exactly the derivative.

slides.heading: Choosing a substitution
slides.body_md: Ask about derivatives first, then about powers.

nodes.label: Is the derivative of some inside part present?
No: is it a power of $\sin$ or $\cos$?
Odd power: keep one factor, $t = \sin x$ or $\cos x$
Otherwise: rewrite, or wait for ch09 methods

visual.alt: Decision flow for choosing a method: if the derivative of an inside part is present, substitute t for that part; otherwise, for powers of sine or cosine use the double-angle identity for even powers or keep one factor for odd powers; otherwise rewrite or use the methods of the next chapter.
visual.caption: Which substitution? Ask about derivatives first.

slides.narration: When you meet a new integrand, ask first whether the derivative of some inside part is present. If it is, substitute for that part. If not, check whether it is a power of sine or cosine and use the plan for even or odd powers. If neither works, rewrite the integrand, or wait for the methods of the next chapter.

slides.heading: Quick check: pick the substitution
slides.body_md: Which substitution suits a fourth power of sine times cosine?
slides.narration: Which choice makes the remaining factor exactly d t?

slides.heading: Integrals of tan, cot, sec and cosec
slides.body_md: All four come from the pattern f prime over f.

visual.alt: Table of the four trigonometric integrals: tan x gives log of mod sec x, cot x gives log of mod sin x, sec x gives log of mod sec x plus tan x, and cosec x gives log of mod cosec x minus cot x, which equals log of mod tan of x over two.
visual.caption: Each is derived by an $\dfrac{f'}{f}$ substitution.

slides.narration: These four results are worth memorising, together with how they are derived. Tan and cot are sine over cosine and cosine over sine, so the pattern f prime over f applies at once. Sec and cosec need a clever multiplier before the same pattern appears.

slides.heading: The graph of the tangent and its antiderivative
slides.body_md: $\displaystyle\int \tan x\,dx = \log|\sec x| + C$ on $\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

visual.alt: Graph on minus 1.3 to 1.3 of y equals tan x, an increasing curve through the origin, and of its antiderivative log of mod sec x, a U-shaped curve with lowest point at the origin; where tan x is negative the antiderivative falls, and where it is positive it rises.
visual.caption: Slope of $\log|\sec x|$ at each $x$ equals $\tan x$.

slides.narration: Where tan x is negative, its antiderivative must fall; where tan x is positive, it must rise. The graph of log of mod sec x does exactly this, with its lowest point at the origin where tan x is zero. Near the ends of the interval both curves grow without bound.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: deriving the integral of sec x
slides.body_md: Show that $\displaystyle\int \sec x\,dx = \log|\sec x + \tan x| + C$.
bullets: Multiply and divide by $\sec x + \tan x$
This is the derivative of the denominator, so the answer is $\log|\sec x + \tan x| + C$

nodes.label: Multiply by $\dfrac{\sec x + \tan x}{\sec x + \tan x}$
which is the derivative of $\sec x + \tan x$

visual.alt: Flow deriving the integral of sec x: multiply top and bottom by sec x plus tan x, the numerator becomes sec squared x plus sec x tan x, which is the derivative of the denominator, so the integral is log of mod sec x plus tan x plus C.
visual.caption: A clever multiplier creates an $\dfrac{f'}{f}$ form.

slides.narration: The integral of sec x is not obvious, but a clever multiplier helps. Multiply top and bottom by sec x plus tan x. The new numerator, sec squared x plus sec x tan x, is exactly the derivative of the new denominator. So the pattern f prime over f gives the answer at once.

slides.heading: Quick check: cot x
slides.body_md: Choose the integral of the cotangent function.
slides.narration: Write cot x as a quotient and look at the numerator.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: a root of an inside function
slides.body_md: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{e^{2x}}{\sqrt{e^{2x} + 3}}\,dx$.

visual.alt: Worked example table: for e to the two x over the root of e to the two x plus three, put t equals e to the two x plus three, so the integral becomes half the integral of t to the minus half, which is root t; the answer is the root of e to the two x plus three plus C.
visual.caption: A root of the inside function is a power $n = -\tfrac12$.

slides.narration: The inside of the root is e to the two x plus three, and its derivative is twice the numerator. So put t equal to the inside. The integral becomes half the integral of t to the minus half, which is the square root of t. Write the answer back in x.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false?
slides.body_md: Decide whether a logarithm answer holds for every real x.
slides.narration: Is the numerator the derivative of the denominator, and can the denominator ever be zero or negative?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Return to $x$ and check by differentiating

visual.alt: Summary flow for Part 2: f prime times a power of f integrates by the power rule, f prime over f gives log of mod f, the four trigonometric integrals come from f prime over f, and every answer is checked by differentiating.
visual.caption: Part 2 in one line.

slides.narration: To sum up. Substitution renames an inside function as t, and its derivative becomes d t. Two patterns cover most problems: a power of a function times its derivative, and a derivative over its function. The four trigonometric integrals follow from the second pattern. Always return to x and check by differentiating.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Use the modulus inside $\log$ unless the expression is always positive

rows: choice of $t$ and $dt$ 1, integral in $t$ 1, answer in $x$ 1
parts such as 2 + 3; label each part and keep "$+\,C$"
forgetting to return to $x$, or dropping a constant factor

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 2: a substitution earns a mark each for t and dt, the integral in t and the answer in x; derivations earn a mark for the rewrite, the substitution and the result; long questions come in parts; common slips are leaving the answer in t and dropping a factor.
visual.caption: Always write the final answer in $x$.

slides.narration: Some final advice. Write down your choice of t and the expression for d t: examiners award marks for both. Take care with constant factors such as one half. Always return to x and add the constant. Keep the modulus inside the log unless the expression is always positive.

notes.title: Indefinite Integrals: Standard Forms and Substitution — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Integration as anti-differentiation
sections.body_md:
If $F'(x) = f(x)$ on an interval, $F$ is an **antiderivative** of $f$, and $\displaystyle\int f(x)\,dx = F(x) + C$. Any two antiderivatives differ by a constant, because their difference has derivative $0$.

- $\displaystyle\int [f(x) \pm g(x)]\,dx = \int f(x)\,dx \pm \int g(x)\,dx$
- $\displaystyle\int k f(x)\,dx = k\int f(x)\,dx$
- A condition such as $F(a) = b$ fixes $C$.

visual.alt: Graph of three parabolas y equals x squared minus 2, x squared, and x squared plus 2, one above another. At x equals 1 they pass through (1, minus 1), (1, 1) and (1, 3), and all three have the same slope 2 there.
visual.caption: Every member of $x^2 + C$ has derivative $2x$: the curves are vertical shifts of one another.

visuals.alt: Table of the profit P of x equals 40 x minus 3 x squared minus 50 for an imagined tea stall at 0, 1, 3 and 5 hundred cups: minus 50, minus 13, 43 and 75 hundred rupees.
visuals.caption: Imagined figures, in hundred rupees; the constant comes from $P(0) = -50$.

sections.heading: 2. Standard integrals and a linear inside
sections.body_md:
- $\displaystyle\int x^n\,dx = \dfrac{x^{n + 1}}{n + 1} + C$ ($n \ne -1$); $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dx}{x} = \log|x| + C$
- $\displaystyle\int e^x\,dx = e^x + C$; $\displaystyle\int \sin x\,dx = -\cos x + C$; $\displaystyle\int \cos x\,dx = \sin x + C$
- $\displaystyle\int \sec^2 x\,dx = \tan x + C$; $\displaystyle\int \operatorname{cosec}^2 x\,dx = -\cot x + C$
- $\displaystyle\int \sec x\tan x\,dx = \sec x + C$; $\displaystyle\int \operatorname{cosec} x\cot x\,dx = -\operatorname{cosec} x + C$

**Linear inside:** replace $x$ by $ax + b$ and divide by $a$, e.g. $\displaystyle\int (ax + b)^n\,dx = \dfrac{(ax + b)^{n + 1}}{a(n + 1)} + C$.

key_terms.definition_md: A result obtained by reading a known derivative backwards.

visual.alt: Table of standard integrals obtained by reading derivatives backwards: power of a linear expression, one over x gives log of mod x, e to the x, sine, cosine, secant squared and cosecant squared.
visual.caption: Each row is a derivative read from right to left.

visuals.alt: Table of four integrands with a linear inside and their integrals: five x plus two cubed, e to the four minus three x, cosine of two x plus one, and one over three x minus four; in each case divide by the coefficient of x.
visuals.caption: A linear inside $ax + b$ costs a factor $\dfrac1a$.

visuals.alt: Worked example table: expand x squared plus one, all squared, over x squared into x squared plus two plus x to the minus two, integrate term by term, and get x cubed over three plus two x minus one over x plus C.
visuals.caption: Checked by differentiating back at four sample points.

sections.heading: 3. Powers of sine and cosine
sections.body_md:
**Even powers** — lower the power: $\sin^2 x = \dfrac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}$, $\cos^2 x = \dfrac{1 + \cos 2x}{2}$; for fourth powers use the identity twice:

$\sin^4 x = \dfrac38 - \dfrac12\cos 2x + \dfrac18\cos 4x$, $\cos^4 x = \dfrac38 + \dfrac12\cos 2x + \dfrac18\cos 4x$.

**Odd powers** — keep one factor: $\sin^3 x = (1 - \cos^2 x)\sin x$ with $t = \cos x$; $\cos^3 x = (1 - \sin^2 x)\cos x$ with $t = \sin x$. The same idea handles products such as $\sin^2 x\cos^3 x$ when one power is odd.

key_terms.definition_md: Replacing a power of sine or cosine by first powers of cosines of multiple angles.

visual.alt: Table of the six powers of sine and cosine in the syllabus: squares use the double-angle identity, cubes keep one factor for a substitution, and fourth powers use the double-angle identity twice; each row gives the rewrite and the integral.
visual.caption: Even powers: lower the power. Odd powers: keep one factor aside.

visuals.alt: Graph on 0 to about 6.3 of y equals sine squared x, which rises and falls between 0 and 1, and of its antiderivative x over 2 minus sine 2 x over 4, which climbs steadily, flattening wherever sine squared x is zero.
visuals.caption: The antiderivative rises fastest where $\sin^2 x = 1$ and levels off where $\sin^2 x = 0$.

visuals.alt: Flow for an odd power of cosine: keep one factor of cos x aside, write the rest with sine using cos squared equals one minus sin squared, substitute t equals sin x, and integrate a polynomial in t.
visuals.caption: The same steps work for $\sin^3 x$ with $t = \cos x$.

visuals.alt: Worked example table for cos squared x times sin cubed x: keep one sin x, write the rest with cosine, substitute t equals cos x with dt equals minus sin x dx, and get minus cos cubed x over three plus cos to the fifth x over five plus C.
visuals.caption: Checked by differentiating back.

visuals.alt: Table comparing cos to the fourth x with three eighths plus half cos 2 x plus one eighth cos 4 x at x equals 0.3, 1 and 2: the two columns agree to four decimal places.
visuals.caption: The reduction is an identity: both columns agree.

sections.heading: 4. The method of substitution
sections.body_md:
If $t = g(x)$ then $dt = g'(x)\,dx$, and $\displaystyle\int f(g(x))g'(x)\,dx = \int f(t)\,dt$. Choose $t$ so that its derivative is present (up to a constant factor), integrate in $t$, then return to $x$.

Useful choices: the inside of a power or a root; the exponent of $e$; the argument of a trigonometric function; $\log x$ when $\dfrac1x$ is present; $\sqrt x$ when $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt x}$ is present.

key_terms.definition_md: Renaming an inside function $g(x)$ as $t$, with $dt = g'(x)\,dx$.

visual.alt: Route map of substitution: spot an inside function, call it t, find dt, integrate in t, and write the answer back in x.
visual.caption: Substitution is the chain rule read backwards.

Otherwise: rewrite, or wait for ch09 methods

sections.heading: 5. The forms f'(x)[f(x)]^n and f'(x)/f(x)
sections.body_md:
- $\displaystyle\int f'(x)[f(x)]^n\,dx = \dfrac{[f(x)]^{n + 1}}{n + 1} + C$, $n \ne -1$
- $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx = \log|f(x)| + C$

If the numerator is a constant multiple $k\,f'(x)$, the answer gets the factor $k$. Drop the modulus only when $f(x) > 0$ throughout (for example $x^2 + 4$, $e^x + 1$, $3 + \sin x$).

sections.heading: 6. Integrals of tan x, cot x, sec x and cosec x
sections.body_md:
- $\displaystyle\int \tan x\,dx = -\log|\cos x| + C = \log|\sec x| + C$
- $\displaystyle\int \cot x\,dx = \log|\sin x| + C$
- $\displaystyle\int \sec x\,dx = \log|\sec x + \tan x| + C$ (multiply by $\dfrac{\sec x + \tan x}{\sec x + \tan x}$)
- $\displaystyle\int \operatorname{cosec} x\,dx = \log|\operatorname{cosec} x - \cot x| + C = \log\left|\tan\dfrac{x}{2}\right| + C$

Each holds on any interval where the integrand is defined.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How ISC marks are awarded**
- *Standard integral (1–2 marks):* correct form, the factor $\dfrac1a$ for a linear inside, and "$+\,C$".
- *Powers of sine and cosine (2–3 marks):* the identity or rewrite, the integration, the simplified answer.
- *Substitution (2–3 marks):* the choice of $t$ and $dt$, the integral in $t$, the answer in $x$.
- *Derivations of $\int \tan x$, $\int \sec x$ (3 marks):* rewrite or multiplier, substitution, result.
- *Section D (5 marks):* questions come in parts such as 2 + 3; label each part.

**Common mistakes**
- Forgetting "$+\,C$" or the factor $\dfrac1a$.
- Using the power rule on $\cos^2 x$ as if it were $x^2$.
- Leaving the answer in $t$.
- Dropping the modulus inside $\log$ when the expression can be negative.

questions.stem_md: Raising a linear expression to a power and integrating: $\displaystyle\int (3x - 2)^4\,dx$ is
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int (ax + b)^n\,dx = \dfrac{(ax + b)^{n + 1}}{a(n + 1)} + C$ with $a = 3$, $n = 4$: divide by $3 \times 5 = 15$. Option (b) forgets the factor $\dfrac13$ from the inner derivative.

questions.stem_md: Recalling which function has derivative $-\operatorname{cosec}^2 x$, the integral $\displaystyle\int \operatorname{cosec}^2 x\,dx$ on $(0, \pi)$ equals
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cot x) = -\operatorname{cosec}^2 x$, so $\dfrac{d}{dx}(-\cot x) = \operatorname{cosec}^2 x$. The sign is the usual trap: option (c) differentiates to $-\operatorname{cosec}^2 x$.

questions.stem_md: Splitting the fraction term by term, for $x \ne 0$ the integral $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{2x^3 - 5}{x^2}\,dx$ is
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{2x^3 - 5}{x^2} = 2x - 5x^{-2}$, and $\displaystyle\int -5x^{-2}\,dx = -5 \cdot \dfrac{x^{-1}}{-1} = \dfrac5x$. So the answer is $x^2 + \dfrac5x + C$.

questions.stem_md: An exponential with a shifted, scaled exponent: $\displaystyle\int e^{3x - 1}\,dx$ equals
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int e^{ax + b}\,dx = \dfrac1a e^{ax + b} + C$ with $a = 3$. Option (a) multiplies where it should divide.

questions.stem_md: For $x > -\tfrac72$, a reciprocal of a linear expression integrates to: $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dx}{2x + 7} =$
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dx}{ax + b} = \dfrac1a\log|ax + b| + C$ with $a = 2$. Option (d) is the derivative of $\dfrac{1}{2x + 7}$, not an integral.

questions.stem_md: Water flows into an imagined tank at Nashik at the rate $V'(t) = 6t^2 - 2$ litres per minute, and the tank holds $40$ litres when $t = 0$. The volume $V(t)$ in litres is
questions.solution_md: $V(t) = \displaystyle\int (6t^2 - 2)\,dt = 2t^3 - 2t + C$, and $V(0) = C = 40$. Option (d) differentiates instead of integrating.

questions.stem_md: Using a trigonometric identity first, $\displaystyle\int (\sec^2 x - 1)\,dx$ on $\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ simplifies to
questions.solution_md: Integrate term by term: $\displaystyle\int \sec^2 x\,dx = \tan x$ and $\displaystyle\int 1\,dx = x$. (The integrand is $\tan^2 x$, but $\dfrac{\tan^3 x}{3}$ is not its integral.)

questions.stem_md: A sine whose angle is five times the variable: $\displaystyle\int \sin 5x\,dx$ is
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(-\dfrac15\cos 5x\right) = \sin 5x$. Both the sign and the factor $\dfrac15$ matter.

questions.stem_md: Lowering the power with a double-angle identity gives $\displaystyle\int \sin^2 x\,dx =$
questions.solution_md: $\sin^2 x = \dfrac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}$, so the integral is $\dfrac{x}{2} - \dfrac{\sin 2x}{4} + C$. Option (b) is the integral of $\cos^2 x$.

questions.stem_md: An odd power of cosine is handled by keeping one $\cos x$ aside: $\displaystyle\int \cos^3 x\,dx$ equals
questions.solution_md: $\cos^3 x = (1 - \sin^2 x)\cos x$; with $t = \sin x$ the integral is $t - \dfrac{t^3}{3} + C = \sin x - \dfrac{\sin^3 x}{3} + C$.

questions.stem_md: Before integrating $\sin^4 x$, which identity reduces the power so that only first powers of cosines of multiple angles remain (after one more step)?
questions.solution_md: Squaring $\sin^2 x = \dfrac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}$ gives $\dfrac{1 - 2\cos 2x + \cos^2 2x}{4}$, and $\cos^2 2x = \dfrac{1 + \cos 4x}{2}$ finishes the job. Options (d) and (b) are false identities.

questions.stem_md: For an odd power of sine, the substitution $t = \cos x$ turns $\displaystyle\int \sin^3 x\,dx$ into
questions.solution_md: $\sin^3 x = (1 - \cos^2 x)\sin x$ and $dt = -\sin x\,dx$: $-\displaystyle\int (1 - t^2)\,dt = -t + \dfrac{t^3}{3} + C$.

questions.stem_md: Using $\cos^2 x = \dfrac{1 + \cos 2x}{2}$, the integral $\displaystyle\int 6\cos^2 x\,dx$ comes to
questions.solution_md: $6\cos^2 x = 3 + 3\cos 2x$, whose integral is $3x + \dfrac{3}{2}\sin 2x + C$.

questions.stem_md: The factor $2x$ is the derivative of the bracket, so $\displaystyle\int 2x\,(x^2 + 3)^4\,dx$ is
questions.solution_md: Put $t = x^2 + 3$, $dt = 2x\,dx$: $\displaystyle\int t^4\,dt = \dfrac{t^5}{5} + C$.

questions.stem_md: Spotting that the numerator is the derivative of the denominator, $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{6x + 2}{3x^2 + 2x + 9}\,dx$ equals
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(3x^2 + 2x + 9) = 6x + 2$, so the integrand has the form $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ and integrates to $\log|f(x)| + C$.

questions.stem_md: Writing $\cot x$ as cosine over sine, on $(0, \pi)$ the integral $\displaystyle\int \cot x\,dx$ is
questions.solution_md: $\cot x = \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$, whose numerator is the derivative of its denominator: $\log|\sin x| + C$.

questions.stem_md: On $\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, the standard result for the integral of the secant function is $\displaystyle\int \sec x\,dx =$
questions.solution_md: Multiplying by $\dfrac{\sec x + \tan x}{\sec x + \tan x}$ gives $\dfrac{\sec x\tan x + \sec^2 x}{\sec x + \tan x}$, an $\dfrac{f'}{f}$ form. Option (d) is the integral of $\tan x$.

questions.stem_md: Which expression is an antiderivative of $\operatorname{cosec} x$ on the interval $(0, \pi)$?
questions.solution_md: Multiply by $\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec} x - \cot x}{\operatorname{cosec} x - \cot x}$: the numerator becomes $\operatorname{cosec}^2 x - \operatorname{cosec} x\cot x$, the derivative of the denominator. Option (c) has the opposite sign (it differentiates to $-\operatorname{cosec} x$).

questions.stem_md: With the substitution $t = \tan x$, the integral $\displaystyle\int e^{\tan x}\sec^2 x\,dx$ on $\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ becomes
questions.solution_md: $dt = \sec^2 x\,dx$, so the integral is $\displaystyle\int e^t\,dt = e^t + C = e^{\tan x} + C$.

questions.stem_md: For $0 < x < \pi$, the quotient $\dfrac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x}$ integrates to
questions.solution_md: The derivative of $1 + \cos x$ is $-\sin x$, so the integrand is $-\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$, giving $-\log(1 + \cos x) + C$ (here $1 + \cos x > 0$).

questions.stem_md: A root in the denominator whose inside has derivative $2x$: $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + 9}}\,dx$ is
questions.solution_md: Put $t = x^2 + 9$, $dt = 2x\,dx$: $\dfrac12\displaystyle\int t^{-1/2}\,dt = t^{1/2} + C = \sqrt{x^2 + 9} + C$. Option (d) is the integral of $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 + 9}}$, a ch09 form.

questions.stem_md: For $x > 1$, the substitution $t = \log x$ shows that $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dx}{x\log x}$ equals
questions.solution_md: $dt = \dfrac{dx}{x}$, so the integral is $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dt}{t} = \log|t| + C = \log|\log x| + C$.

questions.stem_md: A student must integrate $\sin^4 x\cos x$. Which substitution turns it into the integral of a single power of $t$?
questions.solution_md: With $t = \sin x$, $dt = \cos x\,dx$ and the integral becomes $\displaystyle\int t^4\,dt = \dfrac{\sin^5 x}{5} + C$. With $t = \cos x$ the factor $\sin^4 x$ would remain awkward.

questions.stem_md: For $x > 0$, putting $t = \sqrt{x}$ in $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{\cos\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx$ gives the answer
questions.solution_md: $dt = \dfrac{dx}{2\sqrt{x}}$, so $\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt x} = 2\,dt$ and the integral is $2\displaystyle\int \cos t\,dt = 2\sin\sqrt{x} + C$.

questions.stem_md: Choosing $t = 1 + e^{2x}$, the integral $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{e^{2x}}{1 + e^{2x}}\,dx$ evaluates to
questions.solution_md: $dt = 2e^{2x}\,dx$, so the integral is $\dfrac12\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dt}{t} = \dfrac12\log(1 + e^{2x}) + C$.

**Reason (R):** For $x < 0$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\log(-x) = \dfrac{1}{x}$.

**Assertion (A):** $\displaystyle\int \sin^3 x\,dx$ can be found with the substitution $t = \cos x$.

**Reason (R):** $\sin^3 x = (1 - \cos^2 x)\sin x$.

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

**Assertion (A):** On $\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, $\displaystyle\int \tan x\,dx = \log|\sec x| + C$.

**Reason (R):** $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sec x) = \sec x\tan x$.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{2x}{x^2 + 1}\,dx = \log(x^2 + 1) + C$.

**Reason (R):** An integrand of the form $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ integrates to $\log|f(x)| + C$.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.solution_md: Here $f(x) = x^2 + 1$ and $f'(x) = 2x$, and $x^2 + 1 > 0$ lets us drop the modulus. R is the rule that produces A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** $\displaystyle\int \cos^2 x\,dx = \dfrac{\cos^3 x}{3} + C$.

**Reason (R):** $\cos^2 x = \dfrac{1 + \cos 2x}{2}$.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** If $F$ and $G$ are both antiderivatives of the same function on an interval, then $F - G$ is constant there.

**Reason (R):** A function whose derivative is zero at every point of an interval is constant on that interval.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.solution_md: $(F - G)' = f - f = 0$ on the interval, and R then says $F - G$ is constant. This is why every indefinite integral carries "$+\,C$".

questions.stem_md: True or false: $\displaystyle\int e^{2x}\,dx = 2e^{2x} + C$.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(2e^{2x}) = 4e^{2x}$. The correct result is $\dfrac12 e^{2x} + C$: divide by the coefficient of $x$.

questions.stem_md: True or false: on $\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, $\displaystyle\int \sec x\tan x\,dx = \sec x + C$.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sec x) = \sec x\tan x$, so the statement is a standard result read backwards.

questions.stem_md: True or false: to integrate $\cos^4 x$, the double-angle identity must be used twice.
questions.solution_md: $\cos^4 x = \left(\dfrac{1 + \cos 2x}{2}\right)^2$ still contains $\cos^2 2x$, which needs $\cos^2 2x = \dfrac{1 + \cos 4x}{2}$: the identity is used twice.

questions.stem_md: True or false: $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{\cos x}{2 + \sin x}\,dx = \log(2 + \sin x) + C$ for every real $x$.
questions.solution_md: The numerator is the derivative of $2 + \sin x$, and $2 + \sin x \ge 1 > 0$, so no modulus is needed and the result holds for all real $x$.

questions.stem_md: $\displaystyle\int (4x + 1)^3\,dx = \dfrac{(4x + 1)^4}{k} + C$, where $k =$ ____.
questions.solution_md: Divide by $a(n + 1) = 4 \times 4 = 16$.

questions.stem_md: $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\,dx = -\log|f(x)| + C$, where $f(x) =$ ____ (on an interval where $\cos x \ne 0$).
questions.solution_md: With $t = \cos x$, $dt = -\sin x\,dx$, so the integral is $-\log|\cos x| + C$; so $f(x) = \cos x$, that is, cos x.

questions.stem_md: $\displaystyle\int \sin^2 x\,dx = \dfrac{x}{2} - \dfrac{\sin 2x}{k} + C$, where $k =$ ____.
questions.solution_md: $\sin^2 x = \dfrac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}$, and $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{\cos 2x}{2}\,dx = \dfrac{\sin 2x}{4}$, so $k = 4$.

questions.stem_md: An imagined cricket-ball maker in Jalandhar finds that the marginal cost of making $x$ hundred balls is $3x^2 + 2x$ thousand rupees and that the total cost of $1$ hundred balls is $5$ thousand rupees. Find the total cost (in thousand rupees) of $2$ hundred balls.
If $\displaystyle\int 6\sin^2 x\cos x\,dx = k\sin^3 x + C$, find the number $k$.
questions.solution_md: With $t = \sin x$: $\displaystyle\int 6t^2\,dt = 2t^3 + C$, so $k = 2$.

questions.stem_md: If $\displaystyle\int x\,(x^2 + 1)^3\,dx = \dfrac{(x^2 + 1)^4}{k} + C$, find $k$.
questions.solution_md: With $t = x^2 + 1$, $x\,dx = \dfrac{dt}{2}$: $\dfrac12\displaystyle\int t^3\,dt = \dfrac{t^4}{8} + C$, so $k = 8$.

questions.stem_md: $G$ is the antiderivative of $\sec^2 x$ on $\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ with $G(0) = 2$. Find $G\left(\tfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$.
questions.solution_md: $G(x) = \tan x + K$ and $G(0) = K = 2$; so $G\left(\tfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 1 + 2 = 3$.

questions.stem_md: Write $\dfrac{x^2 - 3x + 2}{\sqrt{x}}$ as a sum of powers of $x$ and integrate it with respect to $x$ for $x > 0$.
questions.solution_md: Divide each term by x^(1/2), then use the power rule term by term.

questions.stem_md: Using $\dfrac{1}{\cos^2 x} = \sec^2 x$ and $\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2 x} = \sec x\tan x$, integrate $\dfrac{2 - 3\sin x}{\cos^2 x}$ on $\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\dfrac{2 - 3\sin x}{\cos^2 x} = 2\sec^2 x - 3\sec x\tan x$.

$\displaystyle\int = 2\tan x - 3\sec x + C$.

questions.solution_md: Split the fraction, then use the two standard results.

questions.stem_md: Integrate $\cos^2 x$ with respect to $x$, stating the identity you use.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\cos^2 x = \dfrac{1 + \cos 2x}{2}$.

$\displaystyle\int \cos^2 x\,dx = \dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{\sin 2x}{4} + C$.

questions.solution_md: Lower the power with the double-angle identity.

questions.stem_md: Use $\sin x\cos x = \dfrac12\sin 2x$ and then a double-angle identity to integrate $\sin^2 x\cos^2 x$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\sin^2 x\cos^2 x = \dfrac14\sin^2 2x = \dfrac{1 - \cos 4x}{8}$.

$\displaystyle\int = \dfrac{x}{8} - \dfrac{\sin 4x}{32} + C$.

questions.solution_md: Square the product formula, then lower the power of sin 2x.

questions.stem_md: Integrate $\dfrac{e^x}{e^x + 4}$ with respect to $x$ by a suitable substitution.

answer.model_answer_md:
Put $t = e^x + 4$; then $dt = e^x\,dx$.

$\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dt}{t} = \log|t| + C = \log(e^x + 4) + C$ (as $e^x + 4 > 0$).

questions.solution_md: Numerator is the derivative of the denominator.

questions.stem_md: Integrate $\dfrac{3x^2 + 4}{x^3 + 4x - 1}$ for values of $x$ where the denominator is not zero, naming the form you recognise.

answer.model_answer_md:
The numerator is the derivative of the denominator: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^3 + 4x - 1) = 3x^2 + 4$.

So the integral is $\log|x^3 + 4x - 1| + C$.

questions.solution_md: f′(x)/f(x) form.

questions.stem_md: By putting $t = x^3 + 2$, integrate $x^2(x^3 + 2)^5$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$dt = 3x^2\,dx$, so $x^2\,dx = \dfrac{dt}{3}$.

$\dfrac13\displaystyle\int t^5\,dt = \dfrac{t^6}{18} + C = \dfrac{(x^3 + 2)^6}{18} + C$.

questions.solution_md: Adjust for the factor 3, then use the power rule.

questions.stem_md: On $(0, \pi)$, integrate the product $\cot x\,\log(\sin x)$ by choosing $t = \log(\sin x)$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$dt = \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\,dx = \cot x\,dx$.

$\displaystyle\int t\,dt = \dfrac{t^2}{2} + C = \dfrac{\left(\log \sin x\right)^2}{2} + C$.

questions.solution_md: The derivative of log(sin x) is cot x.

questions.stem_md: A curve in the first quadrant has gradient $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = e^{2x} + \dfrac1x$ and passes through $\left(1, \dfrac{e^2}{2} + \dfrac32\right)$. Find its equation.

answer.model_answer_md:
$y = \displaystyle\int \left(e^{2x} + \dfrac1x\right)dx = \dfrac{e^{2x}}{2} + \log x + K$ ($x > 0$).

At $x = 1$: $\dfrac{e^2}{2} + 0 + K = \dfrac{e^2}{2} + \dfrac32$, so $K = \dfrac32$ and $y = \dfrac{e^{2x}}{2} + \log x + \dfrac32$.

questions.solution_md: Integrate, then fix the constant with the given point.

questions.stem_md: Starting from $\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$, derive $\displaystyle\int \tan x\,dx$ on $\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ and write the answer in two equivalent forms.

answer.model_answer_md:
Put $t = \cos x$, so $dt = -\sin x\,dx$.

$\displaystyle\int \tan x\,dx = \int \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\,dx = -\int \dfrac{dt}{t} = -\log|t| + C = -\log|\cos x| + C$.

Since $-\log|\cos x| = \log\left|\dfrac{1}{\cos x}\right|$, this equals $\log|\sec x| + C$.

questions.solution_md: Substitution t = cos x; then rewrite with sec x.

questions.stem_md: Derive the standard result $\displaystyle\int \sec x\,dx = \log|\sec x + \tan x| + C$, showing the multiplier you use and the substitution.

answer.model_answer_md:
Multiply and divide by $\sec x + \tan x$:

$\displaystyle\int \sec x\,dx = \int \dfrac{\sec x(\sec x + \tan x)}{\sec x + \tan x}\,dx = \int \dfrac{\sec^2 x + \sec x\tan x}{\sec x + \tan x}\,dx$.

Put $t = \sec x + \tan x$: $dt = (\sec x\tan x + \sec^2 x)\,dx$, so the integral is $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dt}{t} = \log|\sec x + \tan x| + C$.

questions.stem_md: Reduce $\sin^4 x$ to first powers of $\cos 2x$ and $\cos 4x$, and hence integrate it.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\sin^4 x = \left(\dfrac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1 - 2\cos 2x + \cos^2 2x}{4} = \dfrac{1 - 2\cos 2x}{4} + \dfrac{1 + \cos 4x}{8} = \dfrac38 - \dfrac12\cos 2x + \dfrac18\cos 4x$.

$\displaystyle\int \sin^4 x\,dx = \dfrac{3x}{8} - \dfrac{\sin 2x}{4} + \dfrac{\sin 4x}{32} + C$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Keep one $\cos x$: $\sin^2 x\cos^3 x = \sin^2 x(1 - \sin^2 x)\cos x$.

Put $t = \sin x$, $dt = \cos x\,dx$: $\displaystyle\int (t^2 - t^4)\,dt = \dfrac{t^3}{3} - \dfrac{t^5}{5} + C$.

So the integral is $\dfrac{\sin^3 x}{3} - \dfrac{\sin^5 x}{5} + C$.

questions.stem_md: Show that $\sin 2x$ is (up to sign) the derivative of $3 + \cos^2 x$, and use this to integrate $\dfrac{\sin 2x}{3 + \cos^2 x}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\dfrac{d}{dx}(3 + \cos^2 x) = 2\cos x(-\sin x) = -\sin 2x$.

Put $t = 3 + \cos^2 x$, $dt = -\sin 2x\,dx$:

$\displaystyle\int \dfrac{\sin 2x}{3 + \cos^2 x}\,dx = -\int \dfrac{dt}{t} = -\log(3 + \cos^2 x) + C$ (no modulus since $3 + \cos^2 x > 0$).

questions.stem_md: For $x > 0$, integrate $\dfrac{1}{x + \sqrt{x}}$ by means of the substitution $x = t^2$ ($t > 0$).

answer.model_answer_md:
$dx = 2t\,dt$ and $x + \sqrt x = t^2 + t = t(t + 1)$.

$\displaystyle\int \dfrac{2t\,dt}{t(t + 1)} = 2\int \dfrac{dt}{t + 1} = 2\log(t + 1) + C$.

So the integral is $2\log\left(1 + \sqrt{x}\right) + C$.

questions.stem_md: Recognise the numerator as related to the derivative of the denominator, and integrate $\dfrac{e^{2x} - e^{-2x}}{e^{2x} + e^{-2x}}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\dfrac{d}{dx}(e^{2x} + e^{-2x}) = 2(e^{2x} - e^{-2x})$.

Put $t = e^{2x} + e^{-2x}$: the numerator times $dx$ is $\dfrac{dt}{2}$.

$\displaystyle\int = \dfrac12\log(e^{2x} + e^{-2x}) + C$ (the denominator is always positive).

questions.stem_md: For $x > -3$, integrate $x\sqrt{x + 3}$ using the substitution $t = x + 3$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$x = t - 3$, $dx = dt$:

So the integral is $\dfrac25(x + 3)^{5/2} - 2(x + 3)^{3/2} + C$.

questions.stem_md:
(a) On $(0, \pi)$, derive $\displaystyle\int \cot x\,dx$. [2]

(b) On $(0, \pi)$, derive $\displaystyle\int \operatorname{cosec} x\,dx = \log|\operatorname{cosec} x - \cot x| + C$, and show that this also equals $\log\left|\tan\dfrac{x}{2}\right| + C$. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\cot x = \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$; with $t = \sin x$, $dt = \cos x\,dx$: $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dt}{t} = \log|\sin x| + C$.

**(b)** Multiply and divide by $\operatorname{cosec} x - \cot x$: the numerator becomes $\operatorname{cosec}^2 x - \operatorname{cosec} x\cot x$, which is the derivative of $\operatorname{cosec} x - \cot x$. Hence $\displaystyle\int \operatorname{cosec} x\,dx = \log|\operatorname{cosec} x - \cot x| + C$.

Also $\operatorname{cosec} x - \cot x = \dfrac{1 - \cos x}{\sin x} = \dfrac{2\sin^2\frac{x}{2}}{2\sin\frac{x}{2}\cos\frac{x}{2}} = \tan\dfrac{x}{2}$.

questions.stem_md:
The slope of a road profile on an imagined ghat section near Ooty is modelled by $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \sin^2 x$ (in suitable units), and the profile passes through $(0, 1)$.

(a) Find $y$ as a function of $x$. [3]

(b) Find the height $y$ at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $y = \displaystyle\int \sin^2 x\,dx = \int \dfrac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}\,dx = \dfrac{x}{2} - \dfrac{\sin 2x}{4} + K$.

At $(0, 1)$: $0 - 0 + K = 1$, so $K = 1$ and $y = \dfrac{x}{2} - \dfrac{\sin 2x}{4} + 1$.

**(b)** At $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$: $\sin \pi = 0$, so $y = \dfrac{\pi}{4} + 1 \approx 1.785$.

(b) For all real $x$, integrate $\dfrac{(1 + x)e^x}{\cos^2(xe^x)}$ (where $\cos(xe^x) \ne 0$) by choosing a suitable $t$. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Put $t = x^2 + 3x + 5$, $dt = (2x + 3)\,dx$: $\displaystyle\int t^{-2}\,dt = -\dfrac1t + C = -\dfrac{1}{x^2 + 3x + 5} + C$.

**(b)** Put $t = xe^x$; then $dt = (e^x + xe^x)\,dx = (1 + x)e^x\,dx$.

$\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dt}{\cos^2 t} = \int \sec^2 t\,dt = \tan t + C = \tan(xe^x) + C$.
